title: How to surpass no-go limits in Gaussian quantum error correction and entangled Gaussian state distillation

predicted_errors.error_location: Definition of covariance matrix preceding Eq. (2)
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The paper defines the covariance entries as "γ(ρ)_{j,k}=tr(ρ x̂_j x̂_k)" while subsequently treating γ as a real symmetric covariance matrix and N as real symmetric positive semidefinite. For noncommuting quadratures this definition is not symmetric or generally real: e.g., tr(ρ q̂p̂)-tr(ρ p̂q̂)=i. The standard Gaussian covariance is the symmetrized quantity tr[ρ{Δx̂_j,Δx̂_k}/2]. Consequently, the stated covariance convention is incompatible with the Gaussian-channel formulas used throughout.

Eq. (13) gives the covariance transformation as "Z_i M Z_i γ Z_i M Z_i + Z_i N Z_i." The right factor must be the transpose of the left transformation matrix. With \tilde M=Z_i M Z_i, Eq. (2) requires \tilde M γ \tilde M^T+\tilde N = Z_i M Z_i γ Z_i M^T Z_i+Z_i N Z_i, not the displayed expression unless M happens to be symmetric. Generic Gaussian symplectic matrices are not symmetric.

predicted_errors.error_location: Lemma 4 and the definition B_i in Eqs. (14), followed by Theorem 5
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The manuscript calls the partially transposed map a Gaussian operation and then uses B_i as an implementable circuit component. Partial transposition is not a completely positive map. In particular, for the beam splitter central to the protocol, the claimed transformed matrix Z_i B Z_i is nonsymplectic, hence cannot be the M matrix of a noiseless physical Gaussian unitary. It therefore cannot be deterministically implemented using beam splitters, squeezers, homodyne measurements, Gaussian ancillas, and feed-forward. A formal covariance-matrix transformation cannot be substituted for a physical channel.

predicted_errors.error_location: Lemma 3 / Fig. 3 claim that swapped CV gate teleportation implements W^{T_i}, and the ensuing beam-splitter partial-transpose implementation
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Lemma 3 is an algebraic vectorization identity involving an idealized maximally entangled object; it does not provide a physical implementation of the partially transposed operator. For a two-mode beam splitter, the partial transpose is in general nonunitary/nonsymplectic. If the asserted deterministic gate-teleportation construction physically implemented it, it would realize a non-CP map, contradicting complete positivity of the stated Gaussian circuit. The displacement recovery of Lemma 1 does not cure this nonphysicality.

predicted_errors.error_location: Abstract; Corollary 6, “Entangled Gaussian state distillation”; Discussion
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The claimed deterministic distillation of "a less noisy shared entangled Gaussian state" from noisy Gaussian EPR states using only local Gaussian resources and classical communication contradicts the Gaussian entanglement-distillation/QEC no-go result invoked by the paper itself. The claimed improvement rests on the nonphysical partial-transpose block B_i. Saying that total entanglement degradation is not decreased does not validate discarding the noisy mode and retaining the allegedly cleaner mode; if the stated physical protocol achieved Eq. (18), it would constitute precisely the forbidden Gaussian-LOCC improvement.

predicted_errors.error_location: Use of |ζ_EPR⟩ and ρ_ζ throughout, especially Corollary 6 and “Finitely squeezed Gaussian EPR” section
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The protocol’s essential resource is an infinitely squeezed EPR state, which is nonnormalizable, has infinite energy, and is not a density operator that can be locally prepared. Thus it is not an available Gaussian resource in the operational sense required by the claims of a practical/local Gaussian protocol. The finite-squeezing discussion does not derive the actual implemented channel or establish that noise polarization/distillation survives finite squeezing, so it does not repair the operational defect.

predicted_errors.error_location: “Application,” Eqs. (15)–(17), especially the sentence following Eq. (17)
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The numerical evaluation is wrong: π^3/(4√(2e)) ≈ 3.324, not 1.012. More importantly, Eq. (17), 1+4/L<e^{4r} with finite L=ln[π^{1.5}/(2σ^4)], is not satisfied for every r>0: as r→0+, the right side tends to 1 while the left side remains strictly greater than 1 when L is finite. Therefore the assertion that the concatenation “always yields benefits for r>0” is false even under the stated noise bound.

predicted_errors.error_location: Appendix G, finite-squeezing fidelity argument after Eqs. (G1)–(G3)
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The text infers high fidelity merely because |tanh(r)|<1 and 1−tanh(r)=o(1), without an error bound or assumptions on W and |ψ⟩. Convergence of the two-mode-squeezed-state series does not justify truncating it. For arbitrary states/operators allowed in Lemma 3, one can choose Fock support at photon numbers far above the effective finite-squeezing cutoff, making the ideal bouncing identity a poor approximation even at large finite r. Thus the claimed finite-resource approximation is not established.

predicted_errors.error_location: References/bibliography at the end of the paper
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The manuscript cites at least 37 numbered references, but the supplied bibliography is absent and replaced by isolated incomplete fragments, e.g. "Proceedings of the 29th annual ACM symposium... pp. 176–" and "tonomous error-correction...". As written, the cited sources—including the central no-go theorem [31] and the claimed GKP result [20]—cannot be identified or checked. This requires correction for attribution and verification.
